blocks.text: 1. Types of RAG

blocks.alt: Naive RAG, advanced RAG, and modular RAG form a progression

blocks.text: Types of RAG surveys the different variations the basic RAG workflow can take, giving a first map of the wider landscape.
It covers the landscape of named RAG variants explored in full depth later in this course.
2. Recapping The Preview
RAG Workflow's closing recap previewed Types of RAG as a survey of the different variations that workflow can take, briefly described there.
This topic gives that preview its complete, dedicated treatment, exploring every detail only briefly hinted at before.
3. Recapping The Basic Six Step Workflow
RAG Workflow laid out steps one through six in full: that six step workflow is the simplest possible version of RAG.
Real systems often modify or extend that basic workflow in specific ways, and that starting point is what the rest of this topic explores.
4. Naive RAG Defined

blocks.alt: A query is retrieved, then generated

blocks.text: Naive RAG refers to exactly that basic six step workflow, run once, with no extra refinement.
Naive RAG, covered as its own dedicated topic later in this course, is the baseline every variant improves on, and it is the first named variant this topic explores.

blocks.text: 5. Preview Of Advanced RAG

blocks.alt: Naive RAG is compared against advanced RAG with query rewriting and re-ranking

blocks.text: Advanced RAG adds refinements like re-ranking, covered generally in RAG Architecture, around that basic workflow.
Advanced RAG, covered as its own dedicated topic later in this course, improves retrieval and generation quality. It is the second named variant this topic explores.
6. Preview Of Modular RAG

blocks.alt: A fixed pipeline is compared against modular RAG with swappable components

blocks.text: Modular RAG treats every component as a swappable, independent building block.
Modular RAG, covered as its own dedicated topic later in this course, allows mixing and matching pieces freely. It is the third named variant this topic explores.

blocks.content: This modular framing connects to the ingestion, chunking, embedding, retrieval, and generation components covered in RAG Architecture, each becoming its own interchangeable piece.

blocks.text: 7. Preview Of Agentic RAG

blocks.alt: Static retrieval is compared against agentic RAG, which decides when to retrieve

blocks.text: Agentic RAG lets the model itself decide when and what to retrieve, a concept covered generally in Agentic AI.
Agentic RAG, covered as its own dedicated module later in this course, adds real decision-making to retrieval. It is the fourth named variant this topic explores.
8. Preview Of Graph RAG

blocks.alt: Flat documents are compared against graph RAG with structured relationships

blocks.text: Graph RAG retrieves from a structured knowledge graph instead of plain, unstructured documents.
Graph RAG, covered as its own dedicated module later in this course, captures explicit relationships between facts. It is the fifth named variant this topic explores.

blocks.text: 9. Preview Of Corrective And Self-RAG

blocks.alt: Standard RAG is compared against self-RAG, which self-critiques retrieval

blocks.text: Corrective and self-RAG add a self-checking step, verifying retrieved content before trusting it.
Both are covered as their own dedicated topics later in this course, adding real, built-in quality checks. They are the sixth and seventh named variants this topic explores.
10. Recognizing Why So Many Named Variants Of RAG Exist
Naive RAG has real limitations. More advanced variants trade added complexity for higher quality.
Naive RAG is fast to build, and it remains the right starting point for simple, early prototypes.
11. Worked Example
The example below compares naive RAG against a simplified advanced RAG with a re-ranking step.

code.content:
retrieved_candidates = [
    ("The office reopens Monday at 9am.", 0.7),
    ("Parking is available on level two.", 0.5),
    ("The office reopens Monday, confirmed by management.", 0.9),
]

def naive_rag_select(candidates):
    return candidates[0][0]  # just takes the first retrieved result, no refinement

def advanced_rag_select(candidates):
    sorted_candidates = sorted(candidates, key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return sorted_candidates[0][0]  # re-ranks by score before selecting

print(f"Retrieved candidates: {retrieved_candidates}")
print(f"\nNaive RAG selection: {naive_rag_select(retrieved_candidates)}")
print(f"Advanced RAG selection: {advanced_rag_select(retrieved_candidates)}")
print("\nNotice: advanced RAG selects the higher-scoring, more reliable passage through re-ranking")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows naive RAG taking the first retrieved result regardless of quality, while advanced RAG re-ranks first and selects the best-scoring passage.

blocks.text: 12. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming all RAG systems work identically, without recognizing these named architectural variants.
Building naive RAG for a production system that needs the refinements advanced RAG provides.
Confusing agentic RAG, where the model decides what to retrieve, with simple, fixed-order retrieval.
Overlooking graph RAG when the underlying data has rich, explicit relationships to exploit.

blocks.text: 13. Key Takeaways

items: Types of RAG surveys the different named variations the basic RAG workflow can take.
Naive RAG is the basic six step workflow, run once with no extra refinement.
Advanced RAG adds refinements like re-ranking around that basic workflow.
Modular RAG treats every component as a swappable, independent building block.
Agentic RAG lets the model itself decide when and what to retrieve.
Graph RAG retrieves from a structured knowledge graph instead of plain documents.
Corrective and self-RAG add a self-checking step, verifying retrieved content before trusting it.
More advanced variants trade added complexity for higher quality; naive RAG suits simple prototypes.
